cues.text: Let us turn now to some additional methods for managing change and for personalising the customer experience.
We will start with one of the most widely used diagnostic tools in organisational change, and then move to how organisations engage and personalise for their customers.
The first idea is McKinsey's 7-S model.
This model assesses seven interdependent organisational elements.
Here they are, in order: strategy, structure, systems, shared values, skills, style and staff.
Notice the word interdependent.
It means that no element stands alone.
If you change one, you put pressure on the others.
The seven elements are often split into two groups.
The first three, strategy, structure and systems, are usually described as hard elements.
They are the ones you can write down, draw on an organisation chart, or find in a policy document.
The remaining four, shared values, skills, style and staff, are described as soft elements.
They concern people, culture, capability and leadership behaviour, and they are harder to see and harder to change.
Among all seven, shared values hold a special position.
The source tells us that shared values influence the rest.

They are the common beliefs about what the organisation stands for and what matters, and they shape how strategy is interpreted, how structures are used, how people behave, and what skills and leadership style are rewarded.
Now consider the example the source gives.
Imagine an organisation adopts a new digital strategy that requires cross-functional squads.
A cross-functional squad is a small team that brings together people from different functions, so that they can work on a product or customer need together.
Now suppose that the structures, the rewards, the staff skills and the leadership style all remain unchanged.
People are still organised in separate departments, rewarded for departmental targets, lacking the skills for squad-based work, and managed in the old way.
The result, according to the source, is that adoption will suffer.
The strategy changed, but the other elements of the 7-S model did not move with it.
That is exactly the misalignment the model is designed to reveal.
The source also introduces agile change management.
This approach uses incremental change, feedback and adaptation.
Rather than imposing one large, predetermined transition, the organisation changes in smaller steps, gathers feedback after each step, and adapts the next step accordingly.
Compare that with a single big-bang rollout that is fixed in advance.
The agile approach lets the organisation learn as it goes.
Let us now move to customer engagement.
The source lists several tools an organisation can use: useful content, communities, social listening, personalised email and support tools.
Take them one at a time.
Useful content means material that genuinely helps customers.
Communities are spaces where customers connect with the organisation and with one another.
Social listening means monitoring what people are saying on social platforms about the organisation, its products and its field.
Personalised email means messages tailored to the recipient.
And support tools are the means by which customers get help.
The source then explains content marketing.
Content marketing attracts and helps customers through relevant information, rather than only sales messages.
So instead of just telling people to buy, the organisation offers information that is useful to them, and that builds attraction and trust.
Next, the source separates three related ideas, and it is important to keep them distinct.
Dynamic content changes website or app elements based on context, behaviour or preferences.
So two visitors might see different banners or layouts on the same page.
Segmentation, by contrast, groups similar users together, so that each group can be treated with suitable messages or offers.
Recommendation engines suggest items to users.
So we have changing content, grouping users, and suggesting items.
They often work together, but they are not the same thing.
The source adds an important caution about personalised communications.
They use relevant context, not simply inserting a customer's name into an email.
Putting a name in the greeting is not real personalisation.
Real personalisation reflects what is relevant to that person in their situation.
Now to the examples.
The source names Amazon product recommendations, Netflix content suggestions and Starbucks loyalty and app offers.
These illustrate different personalisation use cases.
Amazon suggests products.
Netflix suggests content to watch.
Starbucks uses loyalty and app offers.
Please treat these as illustrations of use cases, not as evidence of specific results, because the source does not give us figures.
The source asks us to explain three things about personalisation: the mechanisms, the expected benefits and the constraints.
First, the mechanisms.
There are four: interaction data, segmentation, relevance ranking and feedback.
Interaction data is the record of what users do, such as what they view, choose or buy.
Segmentation groups similar users.
Relevance ranking orders the possible items so that those most relevant to a user appear first.
Feedback is the information about how users respond to what was shown, which lets the system improve.
Second, the expected benefits: discovery, retention and engagement.
Discovery means helping customers find things they would not otherwise have found.
Retention means keeping customers over time.
Engagement means deeper and more active use.
Third, the constraints: privacy, user control, unfair profiling and manipulation.
Privacy concerns how personal data is collected and used.
User control concerns the customer's ability to make choices about their experience.
Unfair profiling is the risk of treating people unjustly because of the categories they are placed in.
Manipulation is the risk of steering people against their own interests.
The source states plainly that personalisation should not become hidden coercion.
To guard against that, it gives four practices.
Explain what information is used.
Respect appropriate choices.
Minimise sensitive data.
And test for biased outcomes.
In other words, be transparent, give people choices, collect no more sensitive data than necessary, and check whether the system treats groups unfairly.
Finally, the worked example.
A grocery app discovers, through journey research, that customers abandon checkout because delivery fees appear late.
Journey research means studying the steps customers go through, and here it reveals the exact point where they leave.
The response has three parts.
First, show the complete cost earlier.
Second, test the change against task completion and complaints, which means checking whether more customers finish their orders and whether complaints fall.
Third, train support staff to resolve fee disputes, because some customers will still have questions about charges.
The source concludes that this improvement integrates customer experience, organisational readiness and process design, rather than only adding features.
The customer experience insight identified the problem.
The process design changed how and when the fee is shown.
Organisational readiness meant preparing the support staff.
Notice how this connects back to the 7-S idea: a real improvement needs several parts of the organisation to move together, not one isolated change.
